For example, twenty states have enacted mandatory legislation establishing state—wide building codes or other standards for industrialized housing, preempting local codes; no such law existed prior to BREAKTHROUGH. The building trades have executed new forms of labor agreements permitting the organization of housing plants as industrial unions and at industrial union rates, with provisions for training and employment of disadvantaged people. HUD program processing requirements are being reviewed to make them responsive to the peculiar problems of industrialized construction. The financial community is being exposed to this housing through the prototype program and through ongoing projects.
And, finally, the individual producers are being assisted in developing projects through an interim program of "set-aside" allocations of mortgage interest housing subsidy funds, for projects which meet BREAKTHROUGH criteria in systems and site design. These Phase III projects are being processed through the HUD Area and Insuring Offices, which are responsible for filing separate, individual Environmental Impact Statements in accordance with normal Department practice.
2. ANALYSIS OF ENVIRONMENTAL CONSEQUENCES
The following analysis of the various environmental aspects and consequences of Operation BREAKTHROUGH, and particularly of the prototype demonstration phase of the program, addresses both the physical and social elements of the program. Operation breakthrough is a complex, and inter-related, program, and the considerations involved in the system development, site plan designs, and site construction were common to all of the Phase II activities. No discussion of specific Phase III sites or activities is included. As noted above, these will be processed on an individual basis in accordance with normal Department procedures.
In the following Analysis, each element is addressed on a programwide basis, except where one or more sites or systems require special discussion. Unless specifically stated to the contrary, examples as given should be considered as typical of the approach taken in similar situations on other sites and with other systems. As noted earlier, specific characteristics of each site and system are provided in Appendix I.
A. Physical Elements of the Program
i. Housing Systems
a) New Materials: Approximately 75% of the residential building in the united States utilizes wood as its basic structural material. However, recent studies have indicated that the lumber supply is limited, and the selected BREAKTHROUGH systems also use concrete, metal and plastic structural systems, with only approximately 1/3 of the systems based on wood products.
